A.explanation: This is about $400 \, \Omega$ too small because it uses $2.000 \, \text{V} - 0.005 \, \text{V}$ incorrectly or miscalculates the driver current.

B.explanation: This adds the $5.00 \, \Omega$ wire instead of subtracting it from the total $800 \, \Omega$ resistance needed in the driver circuit.

C.explanation: A balance length of $40.0 \, \text{cm}$ gives $2.00 \, \Omega$ and $5.00 \, \text{mV}$, so driver current is $2.50 \, \text{mA}$ and $R = 795 \, \Omega$.

D.explanation: This is the total resistance $R + 5.00 \, \Omega = 805 \, \Omega$ and forgets to subtract the $100.0 \, \text{cm}$ wire resistance to get $R$.

hints: Notice the null point is at $PS = 40.0 \, \text{cm}$ on the $100.0 \, \text{cm}$ wire, so find what fraction of the wire balances the $5.00 \, \text{mV}$ solar cell.
At balance the p.d. across length $PS$ equals the solar cell e.m.f., so use the $5.00 \, \Omega$ wire resistance to get the resistance of $PS$ and then the steady driver current $I$.
The $2.000 \, \text{V}$ supply drives that same current $I$ through $R$ in series with the full $5.00 \, \Omega$ wire, so use $2.000 = I(R + 5.00)$ to solve for $R$.
walkthrough: At null the galvanometer current is zero, so the p.d. across $PS$ equals the solar cell e.m.f. of $5.00 \, \text{mV} = 0.00500 \, \text{V}$.
Let the driver current from the $2.000 \, \text{V}$ supply be $I$. Then $I \times R_{PS} = 0.00500 \, \text{V}$, so $I = 0.00500 / 2.00 = 0.00250 \, \text{A} = 2.50 \, \text{mA}$.
The driver loop contains $R$ plus the whole wire $PQ$ of $5.00 \, \Omega$. Hence $2.000 \, \text{V} = I(R + 5.00 \, \Omega)$.
So $R + 5.00 = 2.000 / 0.00250 = 800 \, \Omega$, giving $R = 800 - 5.00 = 795 \, \Omega$. This is option C.
